title: The War Moves East
subtitle: The Ukrainian counterstrokes, a fighting withdrawal and the violence in Lwów
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: In Ukraine, Soviet counterattacks gave way to a fighting withdrawal that continued to complicate German movement. In Lwów, the arrival of occupation brought persecution and violence involving identifiable institutions and participants.
body:
Rain on the roads east

The Southwestern Front’s morning report for 1 July ended with a detail easily lost in accounts of the great tank battles: rain was falling and the unpaved roads were washed out. Above that observation stood the condition of an army group in retreat. The 5th Army was preparing another attack before withdrawing towards the Sluch. The Sixth, Twenty-sixth and 12th Armies were moving through successive positions farther south. Front headquarters had no current information locating the Fourth and 8th Mechanised Corps. The Fifteenth had been reported around Bilyi Kamin. A war often remembered through spectacular tank numbers was being decided by the ability to move exhausted formations along roads that were becoming harder to use. [1] The retreat followed a series of armoured battles around Lutsk, Dubno and Brody. Soviet counterattacks had not destroyed the German penetration or restored the frontier. They had, however, made Army Group South’s progress different from the devastating encirclement achieved around Minsk. German forces were advancing through western Ukraine, but significant Soviet armies remained capable of withdrawing, defending and attacking again. The distinction mattered to both sides. It bought the Soviet command opportunities while leaving it with severely damaged mechanised formations and the continuing danger of a breakthrough towards the old fortified line. [2] [3] Behind the retreating armies, Lwów had fallen to the Germans on 30 June. Soviet security forces had murdered prisoners before leaving. The new occupiers and local collaborators used the discovery of their bodies to incite violence against Jews. On 1 July the city was experiencing a pogrom, making the change of military control immediately lethal for civilians. [4] On 1 July, military withdrawal and the arrival of occupation were changing the same inhabited landscape in different ways. Soviet headquarters were moving from unsuccessful counterstrokes towards a staged withdrawal and a new defensive position. In Lwów, the departure of Soviet authority and arrival of German power changed the conditions under which civilians could be threatened, protected or persecuted. The operational and social histories meet through the movement of armies, but their causes require distinct examination. Soviet movement remained constrained by roads, crossings and damaged communications; attacks against German routes continued despite the retreat. In the occupied city, responsibility for violence must be traced through the institutions and participants involved, rather than absorbed into a general account of military disorder.

Why the southern advance was different

Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South had one principal armoured striking force, Ewald von Kleist’s First Panzer Group. Walter von Reichenau’s 6th Army advanced on the northern part of the Ukrainian sector, while Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s 17th Army fought farther south towards and beyond Lwów. The German plan sought to destroy Soviet forces west of the Dnieper, using the mobile penetration to cut their retreat. But unlike Army Group Centre, Rundstedt did not begin with two panzer groups placed to make a comparable double envelopment around the main opposing deployment. The different arrangement was a constraint on method, not merely a difference in the length of the arrows. [3] Mikhail Kirponos commanded the Soviet Southwestern Front, with Mikhail Potapov’s 5th Army on its northern wing and Ivan Muzychenko’s Sixth around the Lwów sector. Fyodor Kostenko’s Twenty-sixth and Pavel Ponedelin’s Twelfth extended the front towards the Carpathians and the Romanian approaches. These armies were threatened differently as the German penetration developed. Potapov had to contain the thrust through Volhynia and protect the routes towards Rovno, now Rivne. The armies farther south had to avoid remaining too long in the westward projection around Lwów while German mobile forces moved beyond their northern flank. [5] [6] The operational geography was more intricate than an open Ukrainian plain. The Western Bug marked the initial crossing; the Styr, Ikva and Horyn divided subsequent routes. Around Brody and Berestechko, smaller rivers ran through marshy valleys with limited bridges and causeways. The 15th Mechanised Corps’ after-action report listed five significant water obstacles in its intended attack zone and described swampy approaches, restricted roads and commanding ground held by the enemy. Tanks were numerous, but places where they could cross and deploy were not. [7] The southern counterstrokes drew their operational value from the vulnerability of a penetration’s communications. German troops pushing beyond Dubno still depended on routes exposed to Soviet forces to the north and south. Defeating those forces or protecting the roads diverted strength from further movement, imposing costs even where Soviet attacks failed to achieve their assigned objective. That effect should be measured separately from the quality of an attack’s execution and the sustainability of its losses. It explains why German advance could continue while proceeding less freely than the initial plan envisaged, and why the Soviet command still faced a difficult balance between disruption of the enemy and preservation of its own mobile reserves. [3]

The corps that had tanks but lacked a complete force

The counterattack programme described in the study for 25 June required attacks from opposite sides of the German penetration. The Eighth and 15th Mechanised Corps were central to the southern blow; the Ninth and Nineteenth were assigned to Potapov’s northern grouping. The 4th Corps also supplied forces and fought in the Lwów sector. These were substantial formations on organisational charts, but their inventories cannot be added together and treated as the strength of one simultaneous battle. Units arrived at different times, received changing tasks and sometimes operated apart from their parent corps. [8] The 15th Corps offers a particularly revealing case because its commander’s subsequent report explains what was missing. The corps entered the war under Ignaty Karpezo. Its Thirty-seventh Tank Division had an incomplete motorised infantry regiment far from the division and without transport. Some artillery lacked the tractors necessary to move it. The 212th Motorised Division had men but almost no vehicles for carrying them, their weapons or their supplies. Corps signals and engineer units were still being formed and trained. A formation could therefore contain modern tanks while lacking the infantry, bridging and communications needed to make those tanks effective. [7] The corps report places a precise delay within that larger organisational problem. The order requiring an attack at seven on 25 June reportedly reached 15th Corps at 8:30, after the prescribed start. This sequence identifies a transmission failure that an explanation based simply on slow execution would miss. The same account describes marsh-bound movement, artillery arriving from training areas and changes of assembly position. It is retrospective testimony from a command explaining its actions, so its claims require that attribution; nonetheless, the comparison with the front’s dated order establishes a concrete discrepancy between the schedule imposed and the time at which the corps said it received it. [7] [9] Command itself was disrupted by attack. The corps report dates the bombing that incapacitated Karpezo to the evening of 26 June and states that his deputy, Colonel Yermolayev, took over. That dated record is preferable to carrying Karpezo’s name across the entire battle or assuming that a change of commander occurred on the invasion’s first day. German air action mattered here not only because it might destroy tanks. It could wound the people organising a corps, displace its headquarters and consume time needed to coordinate an attack. [7]

The time available to obey

An attack order arriving after its deadline

Front headquarters prescribed a seven o’clock attack on 25 June. 15th Mechanised Corps’ later report stated that the instruction reached it at 8:30 that morning. The two records expose a specific failure in transmission rather than establishing that every subsequent delay had the same cause. They also show why an order’s issue time and its receipt by the formation responsible for execution must be distinguished.

[9] [7]

The counterstroke reaches the German communications

The attack towards Dubno was not wholly imaginary. The Southwestern Front’s report for the night of 27 June states that the 8th Mechanised Corps had begun its counteroffensive from the Radziwiłłów area at nine that morning, with Dubno as its objective by the end of the day. Its leading detachment had passed Sytne at 11.30 without contact with the enemy. The same report located the 15th Corps around Toporiv, reorganising for its own attack towards Berestechko. The two entries show movement and preparation existing side by side, rather than a single coordinated mass advancing in line. [10] A group from Ryabyshev’s 8th Corps, associated with commissar Nikolai Popel and elements of the Twelfth and Thirty-fourth Tank Divisions, penetrated towards Dubno and threatened German communications. Aleksey Isaev’s reconstruction identifies the disruption while distinguishing it from Popel’s more expansive retrospective claims about entry into the city and captured senior officers. German forces, including Hube’s 16th Panzer Division, redirected against the penetration and isolated the Soviet group. The sequence connects achievement and vulnerability: reaching a valuable route imposed a problem on the enemy, while sustaining that position required connections and support the Soviet attackers could not preserve. [11] The 15th Corps’ parallel effort shows why the wider counteroffensive did not develop around that penetration. Its report describes an intended advance of forty kilometres towards Berestechko, across a zone with several difficult water obstacles. The staff considered the available strength inadequate for the assigned task and judged that a narrower attack against German communications was more realistic. Orders to withdraw and then resume the offensive further disrupted the corps’ preparations. These retrospective explanations are partly a commander’s account of failure and must be read as such. They are nonetheless unusually specific about the relation between the task, time and available means. [7] On 28 June, the 10th Tank Division could not force the Ostrivka crossing over a causeway under German artillery and antitank fire. Yermolayev sent a liaison officer to obtain support from the attached 8th Tank Division. The officer’s car was hit and burned; the wounded messenger reached the division through fields and gullies. Two tanks sent on the same mission were also set on fire. The account makes the command problem tangible. Cooperation depended on a messenger physically crossing ground the enemy could already fire across. [7] The Thirty-seventh Tank Division’s difficulty near Stanyslavchyk illustrates the interaction of terrain, fire and coordination. Vehicles attempting to bypass a bridge entered marshy ground and became vulnerable to artillery; the corps subsequently withdrew from the exposed area between rivers. The report’s explanation cannot be reduced to the relative quality of opposing tanks. Crossings channelled movement, supporting arms and messages had to traverse threatened ground, and local setbacks affected the feasibility of the wider assignment. Those relationships explain how a formation with substantial equipment could lose its capacity to deliver an effective blow before every vehicle had been destroyed. [7]

A timetable for retreat, not a recovered front

At eleven on the night of 30 June, Kirponos issued a new programme. The Southwestern Front was to withdraw towards the Korosten, Novograd-Volynskiy, Shepetovka, Starokonstantinov and Proskurov fortified regions by 9 July, while holding an intermediate line until 6 July. The order acknowledged German control of the Dubno–Ostrog–Rovno area after stubborn fighting. It also recognised danger from the north, where German forces had reached Bobruisk, and from concentrations in northeastern Romania. The southern armies were no longer dealing only with the battle immediately in front of them. Their flanks belonged to a widening campaign. [5] The withdrawal was assigned stages rather than a single destination. Potapov’s 5th Army was to begin moving after darkness on 1 July, reach intermediate positions on the Styr and Horyn, and arrive at the Sluch by the morning of the 5th. The 6th Army received its own sequence through Ostrog, Kremenets and Volochisk. The Twenty-sixth and 12th Armies had routes farther south. Mechanised corps were to regroup behind them, and aviation was ordered to protect their movement while continuing to strike the German penetration. These dates establish what the command wanted to achieve. They do not demonstrate that all the intermediate positions were reached or held as prescribed. [5] The morning summary on 1 July shows the first reality against which that programme had to operate. The 5th Army was still combining an attack south towards Mizoch with preparations to withdraw. A German attempt to cross the Horyn the previous afternoon was reported repulsed. The 6th Army was moving through positions east of Lwów, while the Twenty-sixth withdrew from the approaches south of the city. The front could still describe an army-level operation, but it admitted that the whereabouts of two mechanised corps were unknown. This was more coherent than the Western Front’s condition around Minsk, yet far from an orderly march by intact formations. [1] The older fortified regions offered a receiving position only if field forces could make them function as a defence. Kirponos’s instructions required artillery and antitank weapons to be organised around the works, linking the value of fixed installations to the arrival of mobile resources. The withdrawal timetable consequently served more than the evacuation of the forward armies: it sought to create a defended destination before German formations could enter or pass around it. Roads, unloading points and the assignment of reserve formations became part of the same operational problem. A line on a planning map acquired military strength through those arrivals and connections, rather than through its designation as fortified territory. [5] The same order assigned the Forty-ninth Rifle Corps a task distinct from the retreat of the forward armies. Its 190th and 197th Rifle Divisions were to march from Volochisk on the morning of 1 July and occupy fortifications around Liakhovtsy, Bazaliya and Sharlaevka that evening. Kirponos was trying to put troops into the receiving position while the battered mobile formations moved behind it. The corps offered the possibility of a defended destination rather than merely another line towards which exhausted units could be told to withdraw. Whether that possibility became effective depended on arrivals and coordination: the order also allotted separate routes and successive assembly areas to the Fourth, Eighth and 15th Mechanised Corps. Preserving those formations required space on the roads as well as permission to retreat. [5]

A deadline that can be checked

9 July belonged to a Soviet plan

The 30 June order set 9 July for the front’s withdrawal to the fortified regions and 6 July for holding the intermediate line. These are documented benchmarks. They should be compared with later positions rather than converted into a claim that the whole front was safely established on schedule. [5]

For German headquarters, the southern fighting was already a warning against assuming uniform results across the front. Blau’s official study describes repeated Soviet counterattacks and an advance below German expectations. That is a contemporary expectation reconstructed from the German records, not a licence to invent a deadline for Kiev. By 1 July, the Germans had gained substantial ground and defeated the immediate Soviet counteroffensive; they had not destroyed the Southwestern Front in a counterpart to the Minsk encirclement. Both parts of that judgment are necessary. [3]

Lwów’s prisons and the change of occupier

The German capture of Lwów, today Lviv, exposed the bodies of prisoners killed by Soviet security personnel during the retreat. The city’s Łąckiego prison was one site of the murders. Research presented by Lviv’s Center for Urban History dates the beginning of the killings there to the night of 23–24 June and relates them to the Soviet decision to eliminate political detainees rather than permit their release as the Germans approached. The victims of Soviet repression came from several communities. Their murder was a crime committed by the Soviet authorities, and the hurried military withdrawal does not alter that responsibility. [12] The discovery also created an opportunity for German propaganda. Bodies were displayed, relatives searched for missing people, and Jews were forced into the work of removing and arranging the dead. The occupiers and nationalist activists falsely assigned collective responsibility for Soviet crimes to the city’s Jews. Jews had themselves been among the victims of Soviet repression. The political use of the corpses therefore required a deliberate substitution: the actual institutions responsible for the prison murders were replaced by an ethnic and religious population available for persecution. [12] The prison murders and the persecution following their discovery require precise attribution. Soviet security authorities were responsible for killing detainees; German occupiers and participating local antisemites then used the bodies to direct collective accusation against Jews. The second crime exploited the first by substituting an available population for the institutions actually responsible. Explaining this mechanism preserves the victims and culpability of both events. It also prevents the perpetrators’ language of communal revenge from becoming the framework through which the historian describes a sequence of deliberate actions. The political transition in the city was also contested within the invading coalition. On 30 June, Yaroslav Stetsko proclaimed a Ukrainian state in the name of Stepan Bandera’s wing of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists, the OUN-B. The declaration sought to use the German advance to establish national authority. German leaders had their own plans for exploiting and governing Ukraine, and would reject the proclamation and arrest its leaders. Those later measures do not mean that OUN-B activists had been uninvolved in cooperation with the Germans or anti-Jewish persecution at the moment of conquest. [13] The NARA study also reproduces evidence of the organisation’s antisemitic programme. This matters because the persecution was not simply an unplanned emotional response to bodies found in a prison. Existing political ideas, the ambitions of nationalist activists and German occupation policy helped shape the violence. The new state proclaimed by Stetsko was neither a democratic settlement accepted by the city’s different communities nor a government Germany had agreed to recognise. Its immediate history must be understood within those limits. [13]

The pogrom on 1 July

John-Paul Himka’s study of the Lviv pogrom distinguishes the roles of German forces, the Ukrainian nationalist militia and the participating urban crowd. German occupation created the setting and encouraged violence; militia members seized Jews and brought them into the sites of abuse; civilians joined in robbery, humiliation and assault. The crowd included both Poles and Ukrainians. Naming these participants is more accurate than assigning guilt to an entire national population, and it prevents the category “local violence” from obscuring the role of the occupiers. [14] The violence targeted women as well as men and included sexual assault and public degradation. Jews forced to handle the prison dead were attacked under an accusation they could not answer by proving their innocence, because the accusation concerned their identity rather than any individual act. German forces also carried out shootings. Himka’s analysis therefore resists a clean division between a civilian mob and an entirely separate official killing operation: their actions interacted, although particular acts still require specific attribution. [14] The pogrom’s death toll is less certain than its occurrence and perpetrators. The Holocaust Memorial Museum gives at least several hundred victims, possibly more, and warns that familiar totals combine the pogrom with German executions over a longer part of July. Four thousand should therefore not be presented as an agreed count for 1 July alone. Separating those events preserves their chronology without diminishing the crime. [4]

Counting different events

Why familiar totals can mislead

Some estimates combine the early pogrom, prison shootings and later executions. A total for that wider sequence cannot be assigned automatically to the mob violence of 1 July. The event is securely documented even where its exact death toll remains uncertain. [4]

The city’s operational and social histories converge through the transfer of coercive power. Soviet troops withdrew through successive positions while German authorities and local participants acquired the capacity to act against those left behind. Hostility to Soviet rule could coexist with fear of the arriving army, or be exploited to encourage participation in persecution. Neither response can be inferred for an entire population. The evidence must identify the institutions, beliefs and decisions connecting people to particular acts. This preserves both the diversity of experience and the responsibility of those who used the change of occupier to commit violence. [13]

Riga and the unequal movement of the war

Far to the north, German troops occupied Riga on 1 July as Army Group North expanded its position on the Western Dvina. The evening German map shows an advance distributed across several crossings and routes, not one uniform line sweeping through Latvia. The Soviet Northwestern Front’s intelligence report that evening described German concentrations near the river, reconnaissance between Pļaviņas and Krāslava, and movement from the Jēkabpils–Līvāni sector towards Madona and Gulbene. It also recorded air reconnaissance around Tallinn and Pskov. The pressure was spreading beyond the initial river crossings towards the next defensive area. [15] [16] That northern progress should sharpen the comparison with Ukraine rather than draw this study away from it. In the Baltic region, German mobile forces had reached and crossed the Dvina while Soviet armies struggled to reassemble. In the centre, the Minsk pockets were still being reduced as the advance approached another river barrier. In the south, Soviet counterattacks had imposed a more sustained interruption, and the armies around Lwów were withdrawing instead of being trapped together in a great enclosure. The three sectors were parts of one invasion, but they were not keeping the same operational time. [2] The Ukrainian counterattacks failed to defeat the German mobile grouping as ordered, but they imposed fighting for communications and crossings while substantial Soviet armies retained the ability to withdraw. Those consequences belong alongside the damage to mechanised formations that the next defence would need. The operation’s effect therefore has to be assessed through several measures: the assigned objective, the disruption inflicted, the forces preserved and the capacity consumed. That approach explains the different southern tempo without making tank totals or a sweeping claim of salvation stand in for the evidence of what the attacks accomplished. [5] [7] [3] By 1 July, German territorial gains had produced a continuing struggle over the organisation of the next defence and the exercise of power behind the advance. Soviet headquarters sought to connect surviving armies, reserves and fortifications, while civilians faced occupation policies and violence shaped by specific institutions and local participation. Two days later, Stalin’s address would present the emergency to a national audience. The [next chapter](/articles/barbarossa-the-soviet-union-responds-1941-07-03) examines that mobilisation of public purpose alongside the administrative and material arrangements needed to sustain resistance.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. German situation maps and staff reports are evidence of what German headquarters recorded, not an omniscient picture of the battlefield. Soviet operational records are cited from the General Staff’s published documentary collections, accessed in transcription; archival identifiers are those printed in those collections. Orders establish intentions; they do not by themselves prove execution. Postwar military accounts are checked against dated records and identified as retrospective. Place names follow familiar historical usage, with present-day equivalents where useful.
